title: When the Experts Disagree
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos, a reading specialist, defends teaching phonemic awareness with letters rather than as an oral-only activity, drawing on her year teaching half-day kindergarten. She sets her classroom practice against McGuinness's prototype for teaching the alphabet code, the McCandliss word-building study, and the 2024 Erbeli and Rice meta-analysis finding that PA with letters improved reading and spelling where PA without letters did not. She then takes the concerns listed in the 2024 monograph Teaching Phonemic Awareness point by point and answers each from classroom experience, arguing that the activity's goal is better reading, not phonemic awareness as an end in itself. Seidenberg's chicken-and-egg framing supports the claim that phonemic awareness and print knowledge develop reciprocally. She closes by urging teachers to side with data rather than with researchers, and to choose methods that are both effective and efficient. The piece is a practitioner's case for integrating phonology and orthography in early literacy instruction.
points: Combining phonemic awareness work with letters (word chains, minimal pairs) lets one activity build phonology, spelling patterns and orthographic mapping at once, saving scarce instructional minutes.
The Erbeli and Rice meta-analysis is cited as evidence that PA with letters improves reading and spelling beyond what oral-only PA achieves.
Each objection in the 2024 PA guide (unspellable words, letter errors, muddied error diagnosis) is recast as a feature, since teaching the spelling patterns is the point.
Seidenberg's chicken-egg point is used to reject a strict learn-phonemes-then-print sequence in favor of interactive, reciprocal learning.
Teachers are advised to follow the data rather than cheer for researchers, and to judge methods by efficiency as well as effectiveness.
quotes: I was both blessed and cursed to find myself in a completely empty classroom: no worksheets in filing cabinets to distract students with countless cutting and pasting activities; no teacher training in classroom decor to distract me from lesson planning. So what was in my teaching arsenal?

I discovered this research right before my kindergarten assignment and immediately got a copy of Making Sense of Phonics: The Hows and Whys by Isabel Beck, one of the co-authors of the study. The book has lists of words with minimal pairing (shifting by one grapheme at a time: cat, cap, tap, map, mat) to guide my students in making word chains that simultaneously develop phonemic awareness and knowledge of letter sounds and patterns (a union of phonology and orthography), thereby maximizing my instructional time for foundational skills and leaving more time for other literacy components.

Then, more recently, I was thrilled to discover validation for this integration of PA with letters from Florina Erbeli and Marianne Rice (2025 co-recipient of the Rebecca L. Sandak Young Investigator Award presented by the Society for the Scientific Study of Reading) in A Meta-Analysis on the Optimal Cumulative Dosage of Early Phonemic Awareness Instruction (2024). Discussing their research on The Teaching Literacy Podcast, Erbeli and Rice emphasize that both PA with and without letters improved phonemic awareness—but it was PA with letters that improved reading and spelling.

We are teaching spelling patterns and the sounds they represent. Dictated word chains with pay, paid, raid, rain, ray, may, main practice PA and phonics together, especially if we are asking students to say the sound (phoneme) as they write the letter or pattern (grapheme).
If a child makes/writes the word ‘brain’ as ‘bain’, it’s a PA problem. If they make/write the word ‘brain’ as ‘brayn’, it’s a phonics problem. And if they make/write it as ‘bayn’, it’s both.

Teachers rooting for researchers isn’t appropriate in this reading instruction game we’re watching from the stands since science doesn’t choose sides—it chooses data—so we must simply side with the science.
